newsitem.title: USA: Alaska seeks Supreme Court review of compact case.
newsitem.headline: Alaska seeks Supreme Court review of compact case.

text.p: Alaska will ask the U.S. Supreme Court to review a ruling that tossed out a $29 billion claim the state has made against the federal government for its failure to develop vast land tracts here, Gov. Tony Knowles said Monday.

The so-called "statehood compact case," filed in 1993 by Republican Gov. Walter Hickel, argues that the state has been denied minerals revenues that were guaranteed under the act that made Alaska a state in 1959.

"The compact case seeks to uphold the very terms that were agreed to when Alaska joined the union," Knowles said in a news release. "A deal is a deal. The federal government cannot renege on promises such as the state's entitlement to 90 percent of oil and gas revenues."

At the heart of the state's lawsuit is the claim that it is entitled to compensation for oil revenues that, according to state projections, would have resulted from drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and other protected federal lands.
The area is considered a likely prospect for holding large quantities of oil, but the federal government has barred drilling there because of environmental concerns for the wildlife and land.
The U.S. Court of Federal Claims ruled against the state in May 1996, saying the federal government has no obligation to the state to open up federal lands in Alaska to oil drilling.
The ruling also said the 90 percent share of oil and gas revenues was not permanent and could be changed by Congress.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit upheld the lower court's ruling July 8.
Knowles, a Democrat, said the state has hired an attorney in Washington, D.C., to argue that the Supreme Court should review the case.
Also assigned to the case was former Alaska Attorney General Charlie Cole, who drafted it when he served in the Hickel administration, Knowles said.
